messages.subject_clean: C stack running out of memory?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
How can I increase the amount of memory available to iplots?
I'm running it within R on a Linux machine (Ubuntu 10.04). 

I try to keep the number of graphs up to a minimum by calling iplots.off() whenever I don't need a graph. However I think the off() call is not cleaning up graph-related variables in the backend. After trying to plot a few (5-7) plots (say five boxplots, with ~5K datapoints in each), I get an error saying something about a "C stack running low on memory".

I then exit and restart R to start iplots afresh.
In general, how can I manage the amount of memory available to iplots better? Is there a clean-up function?

By the way, I am very new to this package. It's great; thank you very much for developing it!  I've also begun reading the "Interactive Graphics for Data Analysis" book and especially enjoy going through the case studies at the back for basic data exploration. Has been very useful for my work (research on DNA methylation patterns in human health and disease). Seurat is also the only tool I know that allows interaction with heatmaps. Good job!

Regards,
Shraddha
-----
Shraddha Pai
Post-doctoral fellow, Petronis lab
Krembil Family Epigenetic Research Laboratory
Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto

On Dec 2, 2010, at 5:10 PM, Shraddha Pai wrote:

> Hi,

> 
> I try to keep the number of graphs up to a minimum by calling iplots.off() whenever I don't need a graph. However I think the off() call is not cleaning up graph-related variables in the backend. After trying to plot a few (5-7) plots (say five boxplots, with ~5K datapoints in each), I get an error saying something about a "C stack running low on memory".
> 

That has nothing to do with available memory. This seems like an issue with R where it is trying to compute that stack space but that will fail in programs involving Java as each thread has a different  stack base address so the result is bogus. JGR usually tries to disable that check but you may be using iplots outside of JGR (which is not recommended) so the check may be still enabled.

So

a) try using JGR.

b) if you don't want to do that for any reason, you can try to disable the C stack check to see if the issue goes away. To do that, run this before starting iplots (you will need to install the "inline" package first)

stack.off <- cfunction(body="R_CStackLimit = -1; return R_NilValue;",
  includes=c("#define CSTACK_DEFNS 1","#include <Rinternals.h>","#include <Rinterface.h>"))
stack.off()

Cheers,
Simon

> Anyway, here is what I found works:
> 
> (m = matrix(as.double(1:12),3,4))
> [shows m as you would expect]

> (v <- .jcall(jtest, '[[D], 'myfunc', .jarray(m), evalArray=FALSE))
> [shows v = m + 10]
>

> a double[][] and returns a double[][]. It simply adds 10 to every
> element.

The above is plain wrong (well, that's actually a guess since you didn't provide even the signature of the method) - matrices in R are vectors, so the type is double[]. In Java there is no matrix type, so it's up to the application to represent matrices and there are many ways - some more efficient than others. From your example above it seems that you are using double[][] -- so you have to allocate the extra objects one way or another (that's why it's inefficient to represent matrices that way).

But from your e-mail I have the feeling that your questions is rather about calling a method that returns double[][], so for example:
public static double[][] pass();
where double[][] is a rectangular array (i.e. length of all inner arrays is equal).

Unfortunately .jcall is a bit inconsistent due to bug that was introduced with the new J() API. So the intended behavior is (using class Test with the method above):
> J("Test")$pass()
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    2    3    4
[2,]    5    6    7    8
[3,]    9   10   11   12
[4,]   13   14   15   16

The $ operator makes sure that the result is converted to a native R form where possible, including recursive structures like double[][].

However, the intention of .jcall() was to never perform recursive evaluation, so this is intended:

> .jcall("Test","[[D","pass", evalArray=TRUE)
[[1]]
[1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@11ddcde"

[[2]]
[1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@18fb1f7"

[[3]]
[1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@ed0338"

[[4]]
[1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@6e70c7"


The intended behavior (and true in older version of rJava) was for .jcall with evalArray=FALSE to return the reference:

> .jcall("Test","[[D","pass", evalArray=FALSE)
[1] "Java-Array-Object[[D:[[D@8f4fb3"

Unfortunately, the bug is that .jcall uses rJava:::newArray() to create the reference which defaults to simplify=TRUE so the current (buggy) behavior is:

> .jcall("Test","[[D","pass", evalArray=FALSE)
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    2    3    4
[2,]    5    6    7    8
[3,]    9   10   11   12
[4,]   13   14   15   16


The real issue is that:
a) if the bug is fixed, .jcall() can return just the reference which is intended
but
b) there is currently no exposed API for rJava:::newArray so the simplification is not available in any form for references if the bug is fixed (other than using the J/$ API).

That's why I was hesitant so far to fix the bug, but I really should -- which is why the behavior your discovered will change. However, then I need to add some API to be able to convert a reference in the same way that rJava:::newArray provides and expose it - I didn't think through that part, so that's why I got stuck.

I hope it helps...
Cheers,
Simon

messages.subject: Re: [Rd] rJava question
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Dec 28, 2010 at 4:51 PM, Simon Urbanek
<simon.urbanek at r-project.org>wrote:

> On Dec 28, 2010, at 3:29 PM, Dominick Samperi wrote:
>
> > On Tue, Dec 28, 2010 at 2:05 PM, Simon Urbanek <
> simon.urbanek at r-project.org> wrote:
> > Dominick,
> >
> > On Dec 27, 2010, at 11:56 PM, Dominick Samperi wrote:
> >
> > > After some trial and error I figured out how to pass matrices from R to
> java
> > > and back using rJava, but this method is not documented and I wonder if
> there is a
> > > better way?
> > >
> >
> > stats-rosuda-devel is the rJava list you want to use.
> >
> > OK Simon, redirected to stats-rusuda-devel (removed r-devel).
> >
> > > Anyway, here is what I found works:
> > >
> > > (m = matrix(as.double(1:12),3,4))
> > > [shows m as you would expect]
> > >
> > > jtest <- .jnew("JTest")
> > > (v <- .jcall(jtest, '[[D], 'myfunc', .jarray(m), evalArray=FALSE))
> > > [shows v = m + 10]
> > >
> > > Here the JTest class has a method named myfunc that accepts
> > > a double[][] and returns a double[][]. It simply adds 10 to every
> > > element.
> > >
> >
> > The above is plain wrong (well, that's actually a guess since you didn't
> provide even the signature of the method) - matrices in R are vectors, so
> the type is double[]. In Java there is no matrix type, so it's up to the
> application to represent matrices and there are many ways - some more
> efficient than others. From your example above it seems that you are using
> double[][] -- so you have to allocate the extra objects one way or another
> (that's why it's inefficient to represent matrices that way).
> >
> > I am mostly concerned with efficiency on the Java side, not on the
> interface, and double[][] is useful for numerical computations (on the Java
> side), can be used without the overhead of boxing/unboxing (pass by
> reference), and is a native (non-Object) type.
> >
>
> It's not, really, because Java doesn't have native vector objects as it's
> not a vector language. That's why it's up to your routines to use the
> representation you want. But, still, double[][] has the overhead of an
> additional object per row (or column depending on your interpretation) and
> thus is nto the most efficient when dealing with big matrices.
>

Thanks for the tips on rJava Simon. Your comment here leads to a related
question. I have seen studies
that claim Java can compete with optimized C/C++ when the tasks are
well-defined benchmarks that
do not involve a lot of object copying (the Achilles heel of many
object-oriented system). Doesn't this
discount to some extend your comment that Java is not a vector language? You
probably know more
about these studies than I do.

Thanks,
Dominick


> Now, I have to admit that there is another change in rJava which I was not
> aware of and I think it's plain wrong: .jarray(matrix(...))should always
> return double[] but apparently there is some new code that makes it into
> double[][]. It boils down to the fact that dispatch=FALSE should the the
> default in .jarray but is not.
>
>
> >
> > But from your e-mail I have the feeling that your questions is rather
> about calling a method that returns double[][], so for example:
> > public static double[][] pass();
> > where double[][] is a rectangular array (i.e. length of all inner arrays
> is equal).
> >
> > My question was about passing double matrices between R and Java, both
> directions, so the
> > method signature on the Java side would be:
> > public double[][] myfunc(double[][] m) {...}
> >
> > It appears that the tools are there in rJava to solve this problem (as my
> hack shows),
> > but the interface is still in flux.
>
> Well, the .jcall, .jarray tools should NOT touch matrices at all - the fact
> that they do is a serious bug. What is debatable is that using a$foo(m)
> could try to match double[][] for convenience, but plain .jarray(m) must
> return a vector = "[xxx" type.
>
>
> > I am not sure why my hack is plain wrong, as you say. It more-or-less
> follows the docs, except for the fact that I had to peek at the code to see
> that the sense of evalArray is reversed.
> >
>
> As I said - it's both wrong how rJava behaves, not how you interpreted it
> ;). Old versions of rJava behaved as expected - .jarray(matrix(...))
> returned double[] and evalArray=FALSE returned the reference.
>
>
> > is there currently a preferred way to address this problem? Would that be
> to just work with the list of java references and convert to vectors as
> needed using .jevalArray, binding into a matrix if desired?
> >
>
> Well, as-is rJava is broken (I wonder why this didn't show up in the
> dependent packages?) -- the intention was that for returning doubly-linked
> matrices (double[][]) you should be able to do
> sapply(.jcall(x, "[[D", ...), .jevalArray)
> which still works. For passing matrices you can either use double[] as
> input and re-copy in Java (if you need to), or split it up in R (e.g.,
> .jarray(lapply(as.data.frame(m),.jarray),"[D")).
>
> That said, the dispatch=TRUE support can be useful, so you can pass
> matrices in the doubly-linked form, and I will retain it, but I'll revert
> the default to FALSE for compatibility with older versions and the original
> intention. As for retrieving matrices, we'll need some other argument
> because evalArray=FALSE returns simply the wrong result -- for symmetry we
> could add dispatch=TRUE in .jevalArray ...
>
> Thanks for the catch - this really needs fixing - I shall release 0.8-9
> very soon..
> Simon
>
>
>
> >
> >
> > Unfortunately .jcall is a bit inconsistent due to bug that was introduced
> with the new J() API. So the intended behavior is (using class Test with the
> method above):
> > > J("Test")$pass()
> >     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
> > [1,]    1    2    3    4
> > [2,]    5    6    7    8
> > [3,]    9   10   11   12
> > [4,]   13   14   15   16
> >
> > The $ operator makes sure that the result is converted to a native R form
> where possible, including recursive structures like double[][].
> >
> > However, the intention of .jcall() was to never perform recursive
> evaluation, so this is intended:
> >
> > > .jcall("Test","[[D","pass", evalArray=TRUE)
> > [[1]]
> > [1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@11ddcde"
> >
> > [[2]]
> > [1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@18fb1f7"
> >
> > [[3]]
> > [1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@ed0338"
> >
> > [[4]]
> > [1] "Java-Array-Object[D:[D@6e70c7"
> >
> >
> > The intended behavior (and true in older version of rJava) was for .jcall
> with evalArray=FALSE to return the reference:
> >
> > > .jcall("Test","[[D","pass", evalArray=FALSE)
> > [1] "Java-Array-Object[[D:[[D@8f4fb3"
> >
> > Unfortunately, the bug is that .jcall uses rJava:::newArray() to create
> the reference which defaults to simplify=TRUE so the current (buggy)
> behavior is:
> >
> > > .jcall("Test","[[D","pass", evalArray=FALSE)
> >     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
> > [1,]    1    2    3    4
> > [2,]    5    6    7    8
> > [3,]    9   10   11   12
> > [4,]   13   14   15   16
> >
> >
> > The real issue is that:
> > a) if the bug is fixed, .jcall() can return just the reference which is
> intended
> > but
> > b) there is currently no exposed API for rJava:::newArray so the
> simplification is not available in any form for references if the bug is
> fixed (other than using the J/$ API).
> >
> > That's why I was hesitant so far to fix the bug, but I really should --
> which is why the behavior your discovered will change. However, then I need
> to add some API to be able to convert a reference in the same way that
> rJava:::newArray provides and expose it - I didn't think through that part,
> so that's why I got stuck.
> >
> > I hope it helps...
> > Cheers,
> > Simon
> >
> > (PS: please continue any discussion on stats-rosuda-devel)
> >
> >
> > > The parameter 'evalArray' is confusing because when
> > > evalArray=TRUE the result is NOT evaluated (a list is returned
> > > that you then have to apply .jevalArray to do get the answer).
> > >
> > > There seems to be an option to have a java reference returned
> > > instead of the actual matrix. Can the R side manipulate the
> > > matrix (on the java side) through this reference?
> > >
> > > Thanks,
> > > Dominick
> > >
> > >       [[alternative HTML version deleted]]
> > >
> > > ______________________________________________
> > > R-devel at r-project.org mailing list
> > > https://stat.ethz.ch/mailman/listinfo/r-devel
> > >
> > >
> >
> >
>
